utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with Mr. Michael Greaves. Unfortunately, Mr. Mucic is not present in the courtroom today and we do not have his agreement for the continuation of the hearing in his absence. I also ask the court's permission to visit my client in the detention unit, whereas Michael Greaves will stay behind during the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, we are here to represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am surprised to hear Mr. Olujic speaking in the way that he did after hearing the views of the Trial Chamber yesterday. Either he has misunderstood the position of the Trial Chamber, or the position of a criminal trial, or he is particularly ignorant about what the law says when a person is compulsorily on trial. If he is, I suppose, he might reconsider his position to know what to say in circumstances of this nature. The Trial Chamber observes a few things. Apart from the fact that we heard nothing from Mr. Olujic even before this incident occurred, when he knew that this was a stratagem of his client -- he kept quiet -- and merely told the Trial Chamber that things had happened and that his client had not waived his rights -- this is what he told us. Yesterday, Mr. Greaves told us that the main complaint of Mr. Mucic, who has for a long time behaved in this Tribunal as a rascal -- that his main complaint was that Mr. Mucic was not allowed access to his investigator. That is the main complaint -- not the question of his health. After a lot of concentration, we got in touch with the administration which sent someone to interview Mr. Mucic at the detention centre. I will read out to you what transpired: "Yesterday evening (16 April 1998), about 9 p.m. [the party] visited Mr. Mucic at detention unit. He was recalled his right to be present in the courtroom during the Trial, but he was told that the Chamber considers that he waived this right since he had decided unilaterally not to come to the courtroom. He was told that the trial carries on without him. After Mr. Mucic heard this, he said that he does not want to talk without his Defence counsel. He was told that he does not need to say anything. However, he said that he is not in a physical and psychological condition to attend the trial. He was asked about the problems with the investigator and he told that there is a problem concerning the contacts with the investigators, but it is not a main reason for his refusal to come to the courtroom. He repeated that the main reason for his absence is his health and he stressed that it is very painful for him to be in the courtroom the whole day. He informed us that he has no intention to come to the courtroom today. At the end he said that he would consider that this conversation did not take place because one hour ago he took some tranquillisers, so he cannot concentrate. He also repeated that he would wish that this conversation occurred in the presence of his Defence counsel." You are all lawyers and I think you should understand the implications of what has transpired -- it just shows clearly, by any unbiased analysis, a complete absence of good faith in any of the reasons given here. He knows that, if his health was in some disturbance, his counsel could have applied to the Trial Chamber for the necessary assistance. If he had other reasons other than the stratagem to disrupt the proceedings, there would have been a way to discuss with the Trial Chamber how to find a solution. The Trial Chamber has considered it this morning and we do not think it is in the interests of justice to allow this type of situation to continue. Mr. Mucic will have to be brought to this court before 11 a.m. today, by whichever method they can bring him. He should come and tell the court his real problems. The Trial Chamber will rise and we will reassemble at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you can meet him here in the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I ask that your Honours obtain from the Registry the letter which I wrote to them concerning his medical condition so that you are fully informed of that matter as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will discuss that later -- not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will Ms. Residovic call her witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can Enver Tahirovic please be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him make his declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit louder, please? Now I can hear it well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down. ENVER TAHIROVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please introduce yourself by telling the Trial Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Enver Tahirovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, before I proceed with my questioning, I need to advise you of one thing. My questions and your answers are being entered into the record of these proceedings and they need to be interpreted by the interpreters, so that our conversation may be followed by the Trial Chamber and everyone else in the courtroom. I therefore request, Mr. Tahirovic, that you listen to the interpretation coming out of the headset on your desk and only when you hear that interpretation, please answer my question. Also, if you do not understand any of my questions, let me know so I can rephrase it. Is this clear, Mr. Tahirovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When and where were you born, Mr. Tahirovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born 14 September 1956 in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your national group and what is your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim Bosniak, and I am a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now, Mr. Tahirovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession, Mr. Tahirovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By profession, I am a professor of the All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is your education and where did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the high school in Konjic and the faculty of All People's Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not strictly speaking, because I graduated from this faculty, which has the rank of a military academy, so I only had four and a half months of practical training in order to receive my rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold in the former JNA before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you in early April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working as a senior adviser for All People's Defence in the health centre in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you, of late, been on duty in the formation of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am one of the first members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was assigned to the joint command. This was still during the war. However, after the end of the war, in May 1996, I left the army and moved into the civilian sphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, since we are talking about similar names of different entities, can you tell me what joint command did you become a member of and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the joint command of the army and the HVO, which was established after the signing of the Washington Agreement. I became its member in late 1994 -- some time, if I am not mistaken, on 24 December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Currently, I am now the director of the public utility company in Konjic, since October of last year. The name of the company is "Standard".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you were involved in matters of People's Defence in the health centre, I want to ask you whether the health centre in the early April of 1992 was prepared for the wartime activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not say that it was prepared for the wartime conditions, because we did not have enough supplies to meet the needs of the war. It was only on paper -- there were certain plans in case of potential aggression against the former Yugoslavia and then later on against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since at that time you were a citizen of Konjic, and the Trial Chamber has already heard quite a bit about the situation in Konjic, could you now just, very briefly, tell us what was the military strategic important, significance of Konjic and did the shelling at some point start, or combat operations around Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to my training, I had access to quite a bit of organisational material -- plans -- in that period. I know that in all military maps in the former Yugoslavia, the town of Konjic was usually circled with a thick marker, in red, as a very important strategic place, significant for the defence of the former Yugoslavia and the fact that Konjic is in the middle of the canyon of the Neretva River and it linked the Neretva River to the sea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have heard from the two generals about the importance of Konjic, you do not have to touch it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is why I wanted the witness just to confirm that he knew of its strategic importance and I think that I only wanted to elicit two or three sentences about it. I think he already covered that, so I think we need not go any further. So, please, Sir, the Trial Chamber is well acquainted with the strategic importance of Konjic, so I would just like you to tell me if you can confirm this importance and whether at some point the shelling of Konjic started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe all the things that were available in Konjic, but I think you also asked me about the weapons that were there. The Territorial Defence of Konjic consisted of one Partisan Brigade -- that is how it was classified in the former Yugoslavia, which was the 14th Partisan Brigade, which was armed with small arms, infantry-type weapons. It had mortars of 60 and 82 millimetres for immediate support. Then it had some anti-armour equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where this equipment was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the Ljuta barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know under whose control they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, until 1990, this equipment was under the control of the Territorial Defence staff in Konjic, and apart from this, there were also units of Territorial Defence in different companies and weapons of these units, that is, platoons and up to the company, were stored in the various companies. However, some time in the middle of 1990, somewhere around there, an order came that the weapons stored in all companies, as well as the weapons of the Territorial Defence, be placed under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a citizen of Konjic -- and again, please, just a very brief answer -- do you know whether, in April and May, Konjic underwent a blockade and please be very brief because the Trial Chamber has heard this from various witnesses before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Konjic was surrounded by almost all sides. From the south-west, it was not a direct barricade, but Serbs from Donje Selo could easily cut off the highway leading to the coast, and I can tell you -- and maybe no witness has told you this -- but in May 1992 no ambulance, regardless of the kind of a patient, could pass through Bradina to take these patients to Sarajevo for treatment, so that we had to take these patients across mountains -- across Mount Risovica -- we had to take them across very bad roads to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, we have not heard this fact before, but you must be familiar with it because you worked at the health centre. Mr. Tahirovic, since in early April 1992, you were in Konjic, can you tell me who were the leaders with the most authority in Konjic at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody had as much authority as they received votes in the elections of 1991. There was a small concession that was made to the Serbs as far as I know, because they had about 16 per cent share of the population -- of the total population in Konjic, so, even though they were not entitled to it, they were offered the position of the vice-president of the municipal assembly, and Duro Kuljanin, who was the President of the SDS for Konjic, assumed this post . The President of the Konjic municipality was Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic. The President of the executive board was a Croat -- I cannot recall now, and Bruno Jurisic was the secretary of the office for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the TO staff was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the TO staff was Mr. Smajo Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you at some time in May of 1992 come into a situation to join the TO staff and, if you do, can you please explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Mr. Esad Ramic left the JNA and came to Konjic, I met him through some mutual friends. In May he, together with Mr. Dinko Zebic, offered me on several occasions to take over the position of the commander of the Celebici barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you accept this post and, if not, can you state the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I more or less accepted to become the commander of the barracks. However, when I learned that some prisoners, some Serbs, were already being held there, and the citizens of Konjic were talking that these were Serbs from Idbar and Celebici from whom weapons were seized, I refused that post and I stayed in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, nevertheless, in May 1992, become a member of the staff, or some other defence body in Konjic? If you did, can you please explain on whose invitation and what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to the problems that the commander at the time, Esad Ramic, had -- he had a heart condition -- he was brought to the health centre, and we placed him in the room which was the room that I used, because it was one of the quietest rooms around and he needed quiet. In the conversation with him at the time, I had accepted -- I had agreed to accept to become a member of the TO staff and, upon invitation of the new commander, Mr. Boric, on 18 May 1992, I joined the TO staff. At that time, it was already a joint staff of TO and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, on this 18 May when you were invited by Mr. Boric, did you attend a meeting where defence issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a joint meeting of the military structures and the civilian authorities, that is, the war presidency, which took place in the brewery in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, were certain conclusions adopted following this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this meeting, problems of civilian authorities, military issues, and the problems of cooperation between the civilian authorities and military authorities were all discussed. After this meeting certain conclusions were adopted regarding all these issues that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, who was tasked with implementing these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain to you that part of these conclusions related strictly to the civilian affairs, problems with procurement of equipment, and food, and another part of the conclusions related to military matters of the establishment of the then joint command of the TO and the HVO and everybody implemented the aspects of these conclusions that he was charged with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now show you documents which were admitted from the second volume of the expert opinions. It is V-A/7 and may the witness be given these documents so that he can try to identify it. There are enough copies for the Trial Chamber and for my colleagues and the Prosecution. (Handed). I believe it is 244/1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, would you please look through these conclusions? Excuse me, it is a misinterpretation. I see on the transcript it is marked as 244 but it should be 144/1. Mr. Tahirovic, have you looked at the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are those the conclusions of the meeting that you personally attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see from this document what I just said. First, there are matters relating to the civilian authorities, and then I see here -- I forgot to mention this -- this is a very important part with respect to refugees and when somebody got killed, who would bury him and who would be in charge of the burial. It was the Civil Defence that was tasked to take care of this. Then the second part, are conclusions relating to military matters. If necessary, I can comment on each of these conclusions and why they appear here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that will be sufficient for now. As the witness has confirmed the truth of the contents of this document and he personally was present at the meeting that these conclusions were made, and as they are relevant from the standpoint of the Defence, I am tendering them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. They are admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, so Exhibit 144/1. Mr. Tahirovic, will you please tell me, in view of the fact that you have just told us that this was a meeting of the war presidency and the joint command, will you tell me, first, whether you know when the joint command was formed of the HVO and the TO in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A kind of joint command existed from the very beginning, though, in legal terms, at the very beginning of the war, the HVO was not legalised as an official component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, due to its desire to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, it had legitimacy and we treated it as such, that is, we, the citizens of Konjic and probably the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. Some members of the joint command were already working in the pre-war staff of the Territorial Defence, such as, for instance, Dinko Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the course of May, a formal decision was taken to form the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that could have been I think the 12th of May, if my memory does not fail me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. At the meeting whose conclusions you have recognised, was Zejnil Delalic present -- do you remember that? If you do, please tell us. If not, tell us again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember a detail that occurred after that meeting, because my colleague Dzevad Pasic and I had just arrived at the staff headquarters and we were not dressed in uniforms. The commander at the time, Omer Boric, asked Dinko Zebic, his deputy, to dress us appropriately because the HVO already had its uniforms and warehouses and he told him that he would return the uniforms, because Zejnil Delalic was about to bring a convoy in a day or two from Croatia, which would include convoys -- a convoy which would include uniforms so he would be able to make up for those uniforms for him. We went to a village called Vrbice outside Konjic where the HVO had a warehouse and we were issued these uniforms. I do not know whether they were returned to the HVO later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, you have answered my question indirectly, telling us that you learnt that Mr. Delalic was due to come in a day or two from Zagreb, but could you tell the court, with greater precision now, whether Zejnil Delalic was present at that meeting of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, there is no need. We heard your explanation, but not the exact answer to my question and now we have that. Mr. Tahirovic, did you, as of that day, become a member of the TO staff, or, rather, of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether Zejnil Delalic was a member of the staff then, or a member of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Zejnil Delalic commander of the TO staff of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Omer Boric was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long were you a member of the staff in Konjic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By chance and probably because of my familiarity with these issues, I was perhaps the person who spent most time there, with brief breaks when I toured the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, are you telling us that, in 1992, you were, throughout that period, a member of the staff, or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, I was a member of the staff, only I held different positions within the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this fact, Mr. Tahirovic, could you tell us who were the commanders of the TO staff from the beginning until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I jokingly would always say that I was the 7th commander of the municipal staff of Konjic, and I can list the names and you will see what I am saying is true. At the very beginning of the war -- not the war in Konjic but the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the commander of the TO staff was Smajo Prevljak, then Enver Redzepovic took over from him. After that Esad Ramic held that post. After him, came Omer Boric, and then, after him, Esad Ramic came again, and, in October 1992, Mirsad Catic took over the command of the municipal staff and, on 15 January 1993, I became commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From this answer, one could infer the answer to my next question, but let me put it to you all the same. Was Zejnil Delalic at any point in time in 1992 the commander or member of the municipal staff of TO or of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was never even a member and still less a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like the witness to be shown D144/1. This is in the second volume of the expert witness, V-A/27. I have a sufficient number of copies for the Prosecution and the court. (Handed). While this document is being distributed, Mr. Tahirovic, will you please read through the text. Mr. Tahirovic, I will not ask you who issued this document, nor am I asking you to confirm its authenticity, but if you have read the contents, in view of your personal knowledge regarding the position of Mr. Delalic in 1992, can you tell me whether the contents of this certificate are truthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the witness is familiar with the truth linked to the position referred to here and, as this is a document that is of relevance for the Defence case, I should like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already verified it on oath in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And this was in reply to your own question, which is quite a different thing from what he said. He has spoken from his own knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I accept your clarification, but, as the question of the truthfulness of contents was raised during the testimony of the expert witness, that is the reason that prompted me to show the document to the witness and we now have confirmation of the truth of the contents from this witness. So, thank you for your suggestions, your Honours. In view of the position that you held in Konjic, could you please tell me, was Mr. Zejnil Delalic President of the war presidency at any period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was never -- I can assert that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was ever elected to the war presidency of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he ever performed any other duty within the administration of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the government of Konjic, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he held any political post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he lived outside Konjic, so he certainly could not have performed any political function.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As before, without wishing to tender this into evidence, I would like the witness to be shown document D145/1. It is in the third volume, 9th section/1. I have enough copies for the Prosecution and their Honours. (Handed). . Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, I am again not asking you to authenticate this document; I am just asking you whether the facts indicated in this document, according to your personal knowledge, are correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man who signed it -- it is probably his signature and he still holds this position in the municipal assembly, so it can be verified through him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are interested, Mr. Tahirovic, in your personal knowledge regarding 1992 and you have already answered my question, so thank you, the document can be returned to the files. Mr. Tahirovic, do you know what the defence forces of Konjic municipality consisted of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A moment ago, when I spoke about the HVO, I said that the defence forces consisted of the HVO, the Territorial Defence, and the MUP of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when we had these defence forces, were there any other formations in Konjic like the Green Berets, the Patriotic League or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any independent armed groups or Party armies in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking about the city of Konjic or the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Konjic, no; but within the territory of Konjic municipality, there were forces of the SDS -- the armed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, tell me, please, what activities you personally engaged in in the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an officer -- I was an operations man for the educational and training department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities in that department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly staff activities, the drafting and preparation of orders for the commander, visiting defence lines, assisting the commanders in positioning defence lines, and preparing documentation for combat operations prepared for the chief of staff and then the chief of staff submits them to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of these duties that you performed, are you familiar with the way in which combat orders were issued and who signed the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When these combat orders are prepared, for them to be valid for all units, they had to be signed by the commander of the TO staff, that is, the commander of the joint staff, and his deputy, that is, the commander of the HVO headquarters in the joint command -- his deputy in the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we have already admitted into evidence a chart -- an organisational chart of the joint command, I should like to show you -- this is exhibit number 145/1 from volume V-D/10. Could you tell us what is the position that you held on this chart? I have a sufficient number of copies, but I think we already remember the chart from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is one of the aides to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of the aides to the chief of staff. You have the chief of staff, and then below him are the heads of these operations departments and I was one of the officers in the operations department, so we were directly linked to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please place it on the ELMO and show us the position you held, as indicated on the chart?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has explained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You have looked at this chart. Is it truthful regarding the period May/June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I have a little more time, please? Yes, with some minor corrections. For instance, here it says commander of the joint command Ramic and Boric -- in the period when Omer Boric was commander, Esad Ramic was assistant chief of staff for operative and training, so he was my direct superior for a time, and there are some other corrections, but more or less these are the people, but they would change from time to time. Some people were coming and going, but more or less they are those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, could you please tell us which was the superior command to the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the structure of the Territorial Defence, the municipal staffs, as a rule, were subordinated to district staffs. However, because of the situation in Mostar, that is, the HVO would not allow the district staff in Mostar to become operational, we were directly subordinated to the main staff in Sarajevo -- the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to whom was the HVO Konjic subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO Konjic was all the time directly subordinated to the headquarters in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the third defence element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP also had its chain of command, but it would only occasionally join in the defence forces on the basis of a special request, but it was directly linked to the MUP of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown a chart that has not been shown so far. It is a chart contained in D145/1. It is V-D2. I have a sufficient number of copies here. We have it in Bosnian and in English, so please distribute both. (Handed). Have you looked at the chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please place the English version on the ELMO? I apologise. You have already answered a part of the questions that I have for you, so I will just continue. In view of the chart which indicates certain combat units, will you tell us, please, to whom these combat units of Territorial Defence were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this the period when there was a joint command?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the heading -- I am interested in the period April/October, who was in command of the combat units in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the time that we had a joint command, the TO units were under the direct command of the commander, and the HVO units were under the direct control of their commander. The police units were under the direct command of the MUP chief in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your personal knowledge as a member of the command of the TO staff, will you tell me, please, whether this chart is a truthful one -- does it truthfully reflect the chain of command that was in effect for the period April/October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it fully corresponds to the situation in Konjic in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that the witness was a member of the staff and is familiar with this structure and has confirmed the truth of the contents of this chart, I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tahirovic, while you were commander -- no, I apologise -- when you became a member of the joint command -- I am sorry, I am not hearing the interpretation into Bosnian -- while you were a member of the joint command, were any combat operations conducted within the territory of Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I joined the joint command, preparations were already under way for combat operations in Donje Selo and, later, in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you aware whether, before that, there were any negotiations with the armed population on the surrender of weapons and the lifting of the blockade on the roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both in the case of Donje Selo and Bradina, for several days attempts were made to persuade those people to surrender their weapons, so that combat could be avoided, and I am particularly familiar with that situation with respect to Bradina, because the negotiations were conducted in a village above Konjic called Podorasac, and I also know the people on the Serb side who participated in the negotiations at the time. (redacted) (redacted) Another one was my son's teacher in elementary school, Jovo Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell me who signed the order for the combat operation in Donje Selo to lift the blockade on that part of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know -- the order for Donje Selo was signed by the commander of the joint staff, his deputy, and the chief of police in Konjic, because MUP units participated in lifting the blockade of Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the staff of the joint command and MUP took certain steps after this to protect the population in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only then, but at any time we paid attention to the protection of the population in the areas where combat operations were conducted and here I am referring to the population of the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please look at the order, which is contained in document 144/1? It is V-D/1. Can this please be distributed around? I have a question to put to you in that regard. (Handed). My first question to you, Mr. Tahirovic, is: do you know whether any weapons were found amongst this population after the fighting, that is, military weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a part of hunting weapons and quite a number of military arms, that is, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether somebody took these weapons to the staff of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the combat operation itself, commanders of the subordinate units were reporting to us, and they submitted the numbers on the kinds and quantities of weapons that were seized at the time and, later on, by combing the terrain -- this was the task of the military police of the HVO and the MUP, because at that time the TO did not have an organised military police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having reviewed this document, do you remember it from those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said in the beginning, a large number -- not all, but a large number of documents I myself drafted, so I am the author of many of these.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you just stated, this is one of the documents where you pointed out a need to protect the local population of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, of Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a document that the witness has identified that he drafted it and that it was used by his commanders, I ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not have any objection, but the document is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does not bear the name of the person to whom the appointment is made. In fact it appears as if one person is making the appointment but signed by two. I do not know how you can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is also unnecessary -- he has said Donje Selo -- there was a military operation and the area was taken over and a large number of weapons were recovered. He said that -- why have this document? Being in the office of the chief of staff, he should know that an operation took place in Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I am not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was a member of the chief of staff team. He should know a military operation took place in Donje Selo. It was taken over and a large number of weapons were recovered -- hunting rifles and military weapons. Why have this document? He said that. It is something within his personal knowledge, so why bother about the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is no problem here, your Honour. I agree with you -- this is an order of the joint command of the HVO and the MUP, and the provision about protection of civilians is also included here, and through this document I just wanted to point out this fact. Now, whether it is relevant with respect to the superior authority and command, I do not know about that, but the witness did confirm what I have asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why are you putting it forward? It is unnecessary for this purpose. It does not answer any of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. The witness did answer my questions. Mr. Tahirovic, can you tell me whether you know who were deputies of the TO commander, that is, who was the deputy of the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean in the period of the joint command, or regardless of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, answer the best you know -- I am more interested in who was the chief of staff of the municipal staff and who was the deputy commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (INAUDIBLE) who have any relevance to the position of your client in the structure?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that, from the point of view of my client, any elucidation of the structures that were there is of assistance to him. It is something that may be of assistance to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is considerable and consistent emphasis he has no business in the TO, the HVO or any of those organisations -- he was never a member. Everyone you have called have denied it. I do not see how you want to relate him to any of these institutions. I think it is your case -- it is your client. You are entitled to present it the way you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer my question: who was the TO chief of staff, that is, deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when Omer Boric became commander, his deputy was Esad Ramic, and, when Esad Ramic became commander, his deputy or chief of staff was Midhat Cerovac, because while Omer Boric --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Sir, you answered my question. Can you tell me whether the deputy commanders at some period were able to sign certain documents if requested by the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but if specially authorised by the commander, and for the most part that was in cases when the commander was unable to do so, or if there were not very significant documents in order not to overburden the commander, but for the most part, if the commander was absent, the deputy commander could have signed a document on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a question which you did not answer initially, but now it is I think a bit more significant. You were talking about the combat operations, about the lifting of the blockade of Donje Selo, that is, Bradina. During that period, was the town of Konjic subjected to shelling, or were there periods in 1992 when the town was not attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very few days, especially in 1992, when the town of Konjic was not shelled, or when its lines of defence were not attacked and especially during the combat operations this shelling was particularly intense. Sometimes, 200 to 800 projectiles would be lobbed into the town, as far as we were able to count them at some stages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you remembered who signed the order for Donje Selo. As a member of the joint command, do you know who signed the order to lift the blockade of Konjic in the direction of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same persons signed both orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the liberation of Bradina military weapons were found with the population, which had rebelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even later, maybe up to one month later, we were finding additional weapons in this area -- our units did -- and they ranged from hunting weapons to automatic rifles to mortars, 82 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know who was the commander responsible for the combat operations in the area during the Bradina operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Zvonko, Zovko and his command post was -- I do not know if it is really a mountain, but it is a hill over -- above Bradina. It was called Prezlica, which had a very good view of Bradina, and, as far as I know, our mortars were positioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic had any kind of command duty in the operation at Donje Selo or at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not even sure whether he was in Konjic during the operation at Donje Selo, and I know positively that he was not there at the operation of Bradina. I maybe saw him once in town during that period, but I am not even sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During these combat operations, were there any casualties on the part of the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both at Donje Selo and at Bradina, we had two men killed at each of these operations. In Bradina, it was one member of the HVO and one of the TO and at Donje Selo they were both members of the special unit of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know, after these combat operations, whether the persons who took part in these combats and who were found with weapons were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not part of my job, but I know that certain persons were detained after and during the operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these people were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because of the limitations of space, some were kept in the Musala sports hall and some in the Celebici barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which bodies were authorised for detaining these persons and who did the actual arresting and detention of these persons? Also, please tell me whose duty it was -- what body had the duty to detain and arrest these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bodies that would be typically charged with such matters would be the MUP and the military police, and in the case of Donje Selo it was the MUP and the HVO, because the Territorial Defence at that time did not have its own military police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, did you have any knowledge about the fact that some of these individuals were trying to escape to the territory controlled by the Serb forces and whether, even after the operation, there were detentions and arrests of such persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As late as 10, 15, or even more days, there were some arrests, and, frankly speaking, I learned some of these things later from people who were released later. For instance, Dobroslav Djordjic, who had worked with me until the beginning of the war at the health centre, he was captured on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with Dr. Petko Grubac, because he is a brother-in-law of this man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tahirovic, I would like you just to limit yourself to your personal experience -- this would be of best assistance to the Trial Chamber. Let me ask you this: did you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic before the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how, but Zejnil Delalic was somehow on very friendly terms with most of the physicians on the staff in the health centre in Konjic, and I think I met him about five or six years before the outbreak of war through a mutual friend. Dr. Sejo Hajduk -- and I saw him quite often at the health centre in Konjic, and shortly before the war he even brought the dialysis equipment for the Konjic hospital, because it was quite a bit of a health condition in Konjic, I guess, because of the kind of water we had there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Zejnil Delalic in Konjic at the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard at the health centre where I worked that his brother died just before the outbreak of war and that he came to Konjic for the burial of his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, in April, what Mr. Delalic was involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first find out what Mr. Delalic was engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in May, I heard that he was in Zagreb where he had gone to procure some equipment and food, because of the contacts that he had in the Republic of Croatia and in the west. We also knew that his brother was a manager of some kind in Zagreb and that he had a lot of business contacts abroad and that he had gone there to bring some stuff back to Konjic, including uniforms, as I said previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, did you find out at some point that Mr. Delalic was appointed to the position of coordinator and, if you do, do you know who appointed him and what it entailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a day or two after that joint meeting of the war presidency and the joint command, I learned that Zejnil Delalic was appointed coordinator to work as a go-between between the war presidency and the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, was the war presidency superior to the TO staff, or the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At no point throughout the war was the war presidency superior to the TO headquarters, or the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Zejnil Delalic at any time, as coordinator, superior to you or to your staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the laws -- the military regulations that were in force at that time in the area, no civilian could ever be superior to a military person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, did you, in June, take part in preparations for some combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some time in early June, I went to visit my family in Korcula and, when I came, Esad Ramic was commander again, and I heard that preparations were underway for lifting the blockade of Borci and, as an operations officer, I got involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the HVO also take part in these preparations, especially Dinko Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so -- practically up until the last day. May I sort of expound -- not much -- I just want to take you back a bit. The HVO held a very short line of defence around the town of Konjic. It was in the direction of the village of Bijela -- it was kind of a Tactical Group, so they were given this area -- they were supposed to prepare it and, through their connections in Croatia, they were supposed to provide a certain amount of artillery pieces and ammunition and all this was unfolding well up until one or two days -- I think it was one day before the operation at Borci was to commence, because they did not get agreement from their headquarters in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who issued the command for the operation at Borci -- did it have any codename, by the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Borci operation was codenamed Operation Oganj. It was usual that all the operations would be codenamed -- that was the practice throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation with the HVO, can you tell me who was the commander of this operation, who issued the order for the Oganj Operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the supreme command which issued this order for the lifting of the blockade, and the commander of the TO staff was Mr. Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this operation last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 22 June until early August -- maybe a few days into August. That was the time when there was serious fighting, but we left part of our forces throughout August, which engaged in combat operations with the Serb forces. We left some sabotage units there in order to prevent a counterattack from the Serb forces from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, what was your duty personally during this combat operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already stated, for the most part I was a staff officer, and Commander Ramic, due to significant problems with the HVO in Konjic at the time, he had left me as an officer on duty in the headquarters in Konjic and I was given a unit at my disposal, which was accommodated in the motel in Konjic and led by Mr. Seid Padalovic, who had been slightly wounded in the leg during a previous attempt to lift the siege of Sarajevo and could not join us for the Oganj Operation, so he was left behind to assist me should there be any misunderstanding with the HVO, because at that time they already were attempting -- that is, the MUP was trying to have the MUP subordinated to the Mostar MUP and they were part of the Croatian Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tahirovic, this is enough. I am about to move to another area, but this may be a good time for the lunch recess?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will now rise. We will reassemble at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in, I would like to address you, please, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have had an opportunity to speak to my client over the luncheon adjournment and I am instructed to address your Honours concerning what has happened today. The defendant asserts that he is unwell, that during the course of today he has requested on four separate occasions medical treatment, but that that has been denied to him. He asserts that he has been brought here under protest and that he does not wish to be here. He asserts that, during the course of today, he has sought but been refused contact with his legal advisers and, as a result of that, is going to resort to other measures, which I suspect will involve him refusing to take food and so on. Your Honour will know, because I have asked for the relevant documentation to be placed before you, that a doctor has seen him and has diagnosed that he has a medical condition of some severity, so plainly there is a medical problem that he has. He sought medical treatment and, if there is any question over whether or not he is physically fit to attend, that is a matter which ought to be dealt with before these proceedings continue further. If -- and I say this with utmost of respect -- if your Honours decide to continue before that position had been established and it was later discovered that he is in fact suffering from a medical condition today, a grave injustice might be caused by continuing the proceedings in his presence in his present condition. As regards last night's visit to the Tribunal, he complains -- sorry, by the Registry, he complains of two matters. Firstly, that when he was visited, he asked immediately to be spoken to in the presence of his lawyers. The meeting continued thereafter, and, on the face of it, he having requested the presence of his lawyers, the meeting should not have continued. He further protests that he was at the time -- had had some medication and was not in a fit state to be interviewed by anybody. He pointed this out and again asked for his lawyers and that was not done. I am very concerned that this is a matter that should not get out of hand in any way. I am very anxious that the greatest of care be taken before any further step to cajole him or coerce him in any way is taken, because that may prove to be counterproductive. I said yesterday and I repeat again today, that it is desirable that this problem can be resolved in other ways, if at all possible, but I anticipate that there may come a time, possibly during today, when I am instructed and my learned friend is instructed to seek redress either from your Honours or from the President of the Tribunal. I do not want that to sound like a threat to your Honours -- it is not intended to be. I am simply telling your Honours what the position may be during the course of today. I hope that this matter does not get further out of hand. That is my earnest desire, but of course I must abide by the instructions which I am given by my client and put those forward to your Honours as fearlessly as I may and I shall do that, with due courtesy to your Honours. Is there anything upon which I can assist you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, if you have finished, you can take your seat. I am surprised that you could even get up to say these things for so many reasons. I assumed, as counsel, your client was acting under your advice. When you advise your client to stay out of the proceedings and still to reserve his right to be present and not to waive that right, you give no choice to the Trial Chamber other than --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please! I am speaking -- I did not disturb you. When you have given him that advice and you come to the Trial Chamber to tell the Trial Chamber that anybody is coercing him and there are some other ways of dealing with that type of advice by counsel, you may take your objections to wherever you like. The Trial Chamber has both a moral and legal obligation to your client, to the country, and to the universe at large and to all involving the administration of justice. We do not expect a bigoted attitude would compel us to be unfair to the other accused persons. I have read the medical report. If there is any need to make the accused stay away, the doctor would have said it. I think you have a copy -- the doctor prescribed treatment -- pain killers and a corset for the lumbar region and that sort of thing. If these are the remedies and he has taken them, I suppose that should be sufficient for the purposes, but, in any event, that is not the issue. No application was made to this Trial Chamber on medical grounds that the accused was staying away. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, he has to be here. If he does not want to be here, he can nominate his counsel to stay on his behalf, and listen to the evidence. But, when there is satisfactory medical evidence enabling him to stay away, we will respect it, but not for the time being. Forget your threats -- they mean nothing as far as the law is concerned. We are obeying the law which we know and we will obey it to its letter. I think that is all the Trial Chamber wants to say about this matter. I do not want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I really must correct one thing that your Honour has said. Nothing that I have said this afternoon should be construed as suggesting that I have advised my client to stay out of court. That is simply not true and if your Honour thinks that, then I would very, very much like your Honour to withdraw the suggestion. I have not done that; I would not do so, and your Honour is incorrect about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As I said, as a judge sitting here, I do not go into argument with counsel -- normally, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just want to correct your Honour's impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As I have told you, every reasonable inference suggests that that is what has happened. In any event, I said I do not argue with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I really do not want to argue about it. I just want to correct the impression that your Honour may have derived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have had enough of it. Ms. Residovic, will you call your witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Kindly inform him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Tahirovic, have you had a short rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, if you remember, we started talking about Operation Oganj and you testified before their Honours that the commander of that operation was Esad Ramic and that you stayed behind as the officer on duty in the municipal staff in the town of Konjic. Will you please tell me whether, in the course of that operation, was any change made regarding the commander of the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in July, the second half of July, the commander Esad Ramic had a slight injury and he went to Split for treatment and he was replaced by the chief of staff, Midhat Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of more than a month that the operation took, as you testified before court, did you personally go to the area of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After two of our offensives in the area of Prenj Mountain failed, Commander Ramic, some time in the first half of July -- I do not know exactly, somewhere around 10 July, I received orders to go with the unit, a company of about 90 men, to go to the area of Mount Prenj -- to be more precise, a position called Tisovica, and because there was a danger of a breakthrough by Serb forces from that side, and the possibility that they could cut communications between the village of Idbar and the village of Celebici, defence lines had to be positioned between Zelena Kapa and Zelena Glava.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those details were probably very important for the defence of Konjic, but in view of this case and this Trial Chamber, I would like to ask you, Mr. Tahirovic, since you were the officer on duty in Konjic and for a time you also went to the area of combat operations, could you tell us whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic participated in the Operation Oganj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Zejnil Delalic, in the Operation Oganj, held the position of a logistics man at the position Oganj 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where was this position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Vranjske Stijene, and I had contact with him several times by radio link, when he asked me, in connection with uniforms that had arrived a day or two before, to distribute those uniforms, as Major Kevric was not around, that I should distribute those uniforms to members of the anti-aircraft defence, who were supposed to reach Vranjske Stijene, to protect that position and other areas against the possibility of Serb air attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic, at any point in time from 27 June when this operation started until its completion, as you said at the beginning of August, was a commander of that operation, or did he take over a command function in the course of those combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, let me be even more precise. In view of the functions that you had, would it be possible for you not to be aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that should not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were very precise when you told us the dates of this Operation Oganj, but let me go back a little to previous questions, because I did not hear the dates of the Operation Donje Selo and the other operation for the liberation of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Donje Selo operation took place on 20 May and the Bradina operation immediately after this one, that is, on 25 May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, you also said that you know that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was appointed the coordinator between the war presidency and the defence forces. As a member of the staff, can you tell us whether, in that capacity, Zejnil Delalic was authorised to issue orders to the army and to make appointments of military or other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also tell us whether you know if, or, rather, what was the role of the war presidency in the initial period with respect to the choice of a commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the law, or, rather, before the war, the presidency of the municipality would propose the commander and his appointment would be made by the republic staff of the TO, later in the main staff of the Territorial Defence, that is, our supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know whether, in any period of time during 1992, the war presidency had the competence and actually carried out the appointment of commanders of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Appointments -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tahirovic, will you please tell me do you know whether, at some time in 1992, Mr. Zejnil Delalic was appointed to a command military position?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of July he was appointed commander of TG1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the previous commander and where that Tactical Group was based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that. It was Mustafa Polutak and the Tactical Group was based in the area of Pazarici, the municipality of Hadzici, actually in Pazarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, referring to your position in the TO Konjic staff in July, you said that the late Seid Padalovic was with you and who participated with you in the battles at Tinovo Brdo. I am asking you in that connection whether you knew any units from Konjic, while the commander of Tactical Group 1 was Mustafa Polutak, were engaged or subordinated to the Tactical Group and its commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around the middle of June under the command of the late Seid Padalovic, a unit of about 200 men was subordinated to the command of TG1, and it was used in the direction of Pazaric, Tinovo Brdo, Hadzici, when we lost several fighters and, as I said myself, Seid Padalovic himself suffered a slight wound in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, can you tell us, during that operation, when the late Padalovic was subordinated to the command of TG1 Mustafa Polutak, to whom were the remaining units that remained in Konjic subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO units to the municipal staff of the TO, HVO units to the HVO staff and the MUP units to the police station of Konjic -- to the MUP station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you know personally that Mr. Zejnil Delalic became commander of Tactical Group 1 at the end of July. Tell me, please, after that appointment, did Mr. Zejnil Delalic become superior to the municipal staff of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Due to the request that one of the artillery pieces be moved to the area of the Tactical Group, a disagreement arose, so that relations between Tactical Group 1 and the municipal staff of Territorial Defence in Konjic were, throughout Mr. Zejnil Delalic's presence, rather strained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which artillery piece is involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a 130-millimetre calibre gun, because we believed that this would detract from the defence of Konjic if this gun were to be transferred to the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who, in the end, gave you the orders in the municipal staff? The orders for the gun to be moved to Igman and to be placed at the disposal of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received the order from the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether some units, or parts of units, after the appointment of Mr. Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1, were subordinated to Mr. Delalic, or some other commanders in the areas of the fighting for lifting the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to Tactical Group 1, but in the Operation Jug, they were subordinated to Tactical Group 2, which was attacking from Mount Igman in the direction of Trnovo. Our units participated in that operation, the operation of the liberation of Trnovo, under the command of Captain Zlatan Redzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How is it you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally worked on the preparation of those units and their despatch to combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, in this period of time, after Zejnil Delalic's appointment as commander of Tactical Group 1, tell me, the units that were not subordinated to him or to the commander of Tactical Group 2 and remained in Konjic, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean under whose command they were?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see -- the defence lines for the town of Konjic, throughout the war, were never less than 100 kilometres, so that we had constant combat operations and all those units were under the command of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic, which later become the army, as of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, if you remember, before the break you spoke about the fact that, in that period, the municipal staff sought to warn or brief troops regarding the need to respect civilians and other inhabitants and to brief them regarding the rules of warfare. Let me ask you first whether, between the period of mobilisation in April and the beginning of combat, did the municipal staff have time to send troops for special training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the duration of the war, and particularly in that period, we made a point of having a mobile unit, which would also undergo training and which could, at any point in time, assist our units in any particular part of the front. Later on, when we were able to form sabotage and reconnaissance units -- we formed two of them, A0004 and Sejdo's Tigers -- and those units, together with other units, were always trained and prepared for combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tahirovic, in connection with what you have said, would you look at these two documents, since you said yourself that you worked on the drafting of these documents, so could you tell us something about them? These have already been admitted into evidence -- D145/1, third volume, V-D/18 and V-D/20. I have a sufficient number of copies for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These do not seem to me documents linked to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an order on interrogation and a checkpoint. Maybe there is an error, or maybe I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question is not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you still pursuing this -- if you find it has no relevance to the question you asked him...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question, perhaps I did not put it properly, so the witness did not understand me. I wanted to ask you, Mr. Tahirovic, whether, through your orders, regardless of what they referred to, did you repeatedly draw attention to the need for respect of the law and a humane treatment of all persons -- that you gave me more detailed answers regarding combat units but I am asking you whether you are familiar with these two documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only I did not understand the question at first. If your question is whether, throughout the war we even wrote leaflets and gave every fighter when going into combat instructions so that no undesirable consequences should occur, such as looting or mistreatment of civilians, we always sought to respect the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, which I, as somebody working in the health sector, are quite familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, I have given you only two documents that have been annexed to the expert report and my question is whether you recognise these documents as documents issued by the joint command of the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the documents have been recognised by the witness, who has confirmed the truthfulness of the contents, I will not tender them into evidence at this stage, but I think that, in a certain way, they corroborate the views of the expert witness, so I just wanted the Trial Chamber to know that this witness is personally familiar with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are at a bit of a disadvantage. There was discussion of two documents -- we have been given only one, 15 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think counsel is proceeding with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just did not know what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see its relevance of what was said. Merely because he drafted a document means you have to tender it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He might have drafted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not questioning that. I did not have the other copy. I asked counsel could I please have it because I could not follow what was going on. I think Madam Residovic may have the other copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have another copy and I said it was D145/1, and I think that both were shown to the witness, and he has already commented on both documents, which was quite sufficient for the Defence at this stage. I apologise if the usher did not give everyone the other document as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We did not receive copies of the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. At least you have nothing to connect this one -- if you have the second document, let us have it.
