utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I gave the second document just now. I apologise for not having given it to your Honours. I have already mentioned its number. My question to the witness was linked to orders given by the staff regarding strict respect of legality. He has recognised the documents and given his answers, because I would like you to see the documents, because his answers applied to both documents which were in the hands of the witness. At the same time, I must apologise to the Trial Chamber, because I am trying to focus my questions as much as possible, for delaying a little bit, because I am trying to group the questions so as to avoid any unnecessary repetition. Mr. Tahirovic, could you please answer a few questions having to do with the development of the army, or, rather, the Territorial Defence and the army in Konjic itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you not think we have enough material about that already on the record -- the development of the army in Konjic? We are more concerned with the role played by Zejnil Delalic in the area -- nothing more than that. Why burden the record unnecessarily with details which are of no use to us in determining the question of guilt or innocence of your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can ask him about his role as a tactical commander, what connection he had with the TO, you can ask him when orders issued placing all formations under the control of Zejnil Delalic, what that really meant? That is what we are concerned about -- we are not concerned with the formation of the Bosnian army or the army in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understood you well, I am doing my best to present facts to the Trial Chamber, through witnesses who were direct participants, about all the things that may be of assistance when making a decision. You have a certain number of facts before you regarding the position of the coordinator, the development of the army and so on that we have heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That, we have got, and we have also got from him that Zejnil Delalic had nothing to do with the TO, except as a coordinator with the war presidency, or with the MUP. This witness has said that. Unless as a tactical commander he had any role to play in the Celebici camp -- if you can succeed in that, that is your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You should know the scope of the indictment and how it concerns your client.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely, your Honours, what I have in mind and many of the documents tendered by the Prosecutor, which you consider to be relevant -- in order for you to be able to know whether they are relevant or not, an eye-witness of these events must tell you what he knows about these things. If you know how the various companies were formed, perhaps you will be able to decide. I cannot testify on behalf of the witness, as you know very well. Perhaps this witness knows how the organisation in Konjic was formed and this may give you a better insight to be able to decide whether any stage existed or not at all that you have heard about. We want you to know the facts, but of course it is up to you to judge those facts. That is my approach to the presentation of my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You might help us better if you can tell us, when TG1 was formed, how he got his own men for the TG1, and how they were deployed, and how they affected the Celebici prison and areas in which he was charged to be responsible. These are the things that are of concern -- whether there were people who remained in the territory has nothing to do with it. The composition of the membership of TG1 and their deployment is what concerns us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (INAUDIBLE) of the Celebici camp came under the TG1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have not heard any evidence to that effect. That is why I am asking these witnesses about what they know. Your Honours, the indictment does not charge my client as the commander of Tactical Group 1, but, rather, that from the end of May he coordinated the forces of the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims and that, as a coordinator and later as commander of Tactical Group 1, was a person of superior authority. Therefore, the scope of the indictment is so broad that the Defence cannot narrow down the presentation of facts for you to be able to rule whether that is so or not. That is all I am trying to say. The indictment has not -- does not allow me to be more concise. The indictment is broad and that is why I have to present my case in such a way, too, that you are able to make your judgement. It is much simpler for me to ask the witness whether he entered hangar 6 or did not. The indictment is very broad in scope regarding my client. I had more than 100 questions -- I have already skipped over 40 so as not to confuse you, but there are some essential things that I think I have to ask this witness. Thank you. I also have a responsibility towards the witness and particularly towards the Trial Chamber, so, please, be very brief and tell the Trial Chamber very briefly, from the moment of mobilisation, how the forces of Territorial Defence in Konjic were organised, so please be concise and clear for the benefit of all of us, as we are not all military men here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we started from detachments on the left- and right-hand of Neretva. This developed into Konjic 1 and Konjic 2, then battalions started to be formed and, in August, there was an attempt to form a brigade, the 111th Brigade of Konjic. However, that attempt failed. It was successful, however, in November, when we succeeded in forming brigades in the territory around Konjic, and that was also the time when the corps was established, and thereby the process of formation of the army in the area of Herzegovina was completed. But the municipal staff remained in effect until 8 January 1994 -- it remained operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think you have indeed been concise and clear at least as far as I am concerned, but, in the process of development from detachments through battalions to brigades, was there a stage of development of the Territorial Defence or the army that could have been called a "coordinator" stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A coordinator stage in the development of the army means nothing. As such, it did not exist. A coordinator is something done by the civilian authority to facilitate contact with us, because we did not have the necessary resources. We did not have our own warehouses, we needed a coordinator to assist us with supplies and logistics -- because we did not have money, either, so gradually this developed and in the second half of the war we reached a stage when we were able to have our own warehouses and when a unit would be issued equipment upon its own request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you earlier on, and now I understand, that a coordinator is no "stage", but, as Mr. Delalic was appointed by the war presidency a coordinator, did he have the authority to issue orders to the army, or to appoint other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how the word "coordinator" is understood here, but, for us, it was easy to understand. It is a person who coordinates, who assists, who bridges between two points, linking certain structures, and all through the war we had some kind of coordinators. If I may, for instance, in a stage when I was a commander, because there was no possibility of coordination, we agreed that, as we already had two brigades and the staff, we, once a week, had meetings at which we would review our problems, distribute resources, so we either had to meet, or somebody had to link these activities. Because of the combat operations we needed to have someone who would link all this together, and make it possible for us to perform our basic duties and to carry out our fundamental tasks and those were the defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The municipality, did it have obligations and responsibilities in the preparation of combat operations, to assist you with logistics and in other ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no other source. We did not have depots. As you probably know, all our warehouses and armament were destroyed and we did not have food storage space, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is not the way that I should put this question, but the coordinator did not have any right to issue orders to military bodies; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did understand me well -- he had no right to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, when we discussed the liberation of Bradina, you told us that you know, even though that is not within your area of responsibility, that some of the persons arrested were detained in Musala and some in the Celebici barracks. Can you please tell me whether you know who decided, and why, to put these persons in that particular place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, because it was their obligation to detain, then it must have been their responsibility, too, the HVO and the MUP. As I said, some of them were already there. That is the reason why I did not agree to be commander of the barracks, because in part of the barracks, there was a prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these persons were detained, did you know as a member of the TO staff that an investigating commission had been established which was supposed to investigate the treatment of these detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that this commission had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was its President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Goran Lokas, who, at that time, was the security officer in the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any report in the staff from this commission about the treatment of the interrogated persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, see any report regarding the problems which the investigating commission encountered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out, that is, did someone tell you anything about some alleged mistreatment of the prisoners at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, from what I know, many citizens of Konjic complained that they were treated almost better than they were -- they were eating the same food, they were protected from shelling, they did nothing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, you answered my question, you have no knowledge of that, but, Mr. Tahirovic, regarding 18 May, that is the date when you started working in the joint command, from that date on until November 1992, did you have any personal communication or contact with persons who either visited the prison or who may have told you something about the prison? Let me be more specific. Did you contact, in the month of June, or did you learn in the month of June that some journalists were expressing an interest to visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, President Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic informed me certain Arabic journalists expressed a wish to visit the prison. I told him that there would be no problem in doing that, but that I wanted to consult with my commander, and, following consultation with my commander, we determined that there were no problems involved in that, and I really do not know whether these journalists did pay a visit there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you ever heard of any person, or did you ever know a person who was detained at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew several individuals, but throughout that period of their detention, I intervened on only one occasion -- intervened on behalf of one of the persons, and I talked to Sadik Dzumhur, called Diksa and he gave me some information that someone from the family of the MUP members, who were killed, wanted to do harm to Miro Golubovic and the sister of Miro Golubovic worked with my wife and I knew them well, so I got in touch with Cerovac, who at that time had taken over the command from Mr. Ramic, and he told me that there was no problem there, that I should only send him certain forms to his command post, which I did, and I know that Mr. Miro was released after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, did you personally ever enter, or did you come near the premises where the prisoners were being kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Celebici several times, but I always went just over to these tunnels. I see that there is a model of Celebici there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point to us where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the gate. I was going down this road (witness indicates on the model with pointer) and I went to these tunnels and there was an ammunition warehouse there -- an ammunition depot. I am sorry, I guess nobody can hear, so my apologies -- I forgot about the microphone. I took this upper road and came to these two tunnels. There was equipment being kept there of the municipal headquarters -- supplies equipment and ammunition and this is where we would take our supplies and this is from where we would send them to the lines of defence (witness indicates with pointer on model) and it was only on one occasion -- I believe that this was an OSCE team, so it was only then that I came to Celebici on orders of Commander Ramic -- I believe this was in August. I went both to Celebici and to Musala, and Major Kevric also accompanied us also, on the orders of Commander Ramic, and then we took this lower road (witness indicates with pointer on model) and we went to the structure, the hangar marked with the letter "E" and that is where the prisoners were kept. When we brought these gentlemen from the OSCE, once we were there, they asked us to step outside of the hangar so that they could talk to the prisoners alone, which we did. Then the same procedure took place at Musala, except that Major Kevric did not go there with me; I went there alone with the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, when you brought this commission, you do not recall exactly whether this was OSCE or whatever it was, but did you go into the hangar 6 and did you see in what condition these detained persons were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I told you, we came inside and the prisoners were lined up. Behind them were blankets and they stood in front of them -- lined up around the walls of the hangar, we stayed there a very short time and then we stepped out and, if I may add, the driver who brought these gentlemen, he said, "Look at them, the way they look, like actors. You should see how our own look like."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So who was this driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He I think was the driver of the HVO police from Mostar, I believe -- not a driver; it was like an escort. They had escorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this commission ask you about the prison authorities or the persons responsible for these detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a brief meeting in our command headquarters, and I do not know, but personally I was not asked this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When they finished the visit, did they tell you what impressions they had, or did they tell you anything or how did you understand whether this delegation was satisfied or not -- but let me not ask you too much; what did this delegation tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not say anything, but, based on their expressions on their faces, they seemed to be very happy with what they found, both at Celebici and at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you entered the hangar at that time, can you tell me, did the prisoners have blankets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I explained, the blankets were lined up against the walls of the hangars and the prisoners were standing in front of these blankets, also lined up all along the walls and so the blankets were behind them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, let me go back to some issues that the Trial Chamber is paying particular attention to. You mentioned that you intervened on behalf of Miro Golubovic -- that was an unusual way, out of the ordinary way of effecting release of certain prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the period of time when Zejnil Delalic was a coordinator, before he became a commander of the TG, as a coordinator, do you know whether Zejnil Delalic had any position of superiority regarding the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he could not have had one, as far as I know, so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, since the Trial Chamber is directing us to clarify the issue of the Tactical Group, how many soldiers from Konjic were subordinated to these Tactical Groups 1 and 2, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not the case throughout this time. I think it was just, for instance, for the Operation South -- Operation Jug -- I think there was one company which was assigned to it and, from what I know, it was the only time, and they were assigned to the Tactical Group 2, which was engaged in an attempt to liberate the town of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You gave us a sufficient explanation regarding the late Mr. Padalovic and I am not going to go back to that, but let me ask you this,

utterances.speaker: MR. TAHIROVIC
utterances.text: was any soldier belonging to Tactical Group 1, whose commander was Mr. Zejnil Delalic -- were any of these soldiers on the staff of the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be that you may not know? Do you know any person from the Celebici prison who was a soldier of the Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe no soldiers were members of the Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not even during the period when Mr. Polutak was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know, did the Tactical Group 1 have any authority over the prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Tactical Group is a provisional formation. It is established only to carry out certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know what the task of the Tactical Group 1 was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. It was the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo from the direction of Hadzici -- that is what we called this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, were you ever a soldier of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the command of the Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, do you know anything about the activities of the court in Konjic; did the court in Konjic work at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not working. We kept insisting on the court being made operational, but they were not in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this was the reason why your staff contacted the supreme command staff, in order to move the prisoners to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. We got in touch with the staff of the supreme command. We asked that the prisoners from Celebici be transferred, either to Zenica or Mostar, and it was suggested to us that we move them to Zenica. However, for objective reasons, that is because of the HVO, we could not transfer them either to Zenica or to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, let us clarify this. How did the group, that is the territorial army, how did you exercise control over the prisons, that is, moving prisoners to somewhere else -- how did you get to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tried, through the supreme command staff, to resolve the issue of the Celebici prisoners -- to use either buses or trucks, and then to transport them to Zenica, because Zenica had a large district prison facility where these persons could be housed, and where appropriate investigation could be conducted, as well as appropriate trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From whom did you take over control -- who was organising or controlling the prisons at the time that you took over this duty, to transfer the prisoners to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not take over the duty to transport the prisoners. These prisoners were a ballast to us in Konjic, because we ourselves did not have enough food at that time, and we could not provide them with adequate accommodation or conditions of life that we thought that they ought to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who was looking after them at the time you stepped into it, to transfer them to somewhere else? Were they just there alone, abandoned and nobody was looking after them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know to what degree you are understanding what I am saying. We did not go there; we asked, in writing, of the command to have them transferred. At that time, the security of the Celebici prison was provided by the Territorial Defence forces. They kept changing. For a while, it was the HVO, for the while it was the MUP and then it was the TO, so at that time we were the ones providing security for the entire Celebici compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There was a time when the Territorial Defence was controlling the Celebici prison -- you were in control at some point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received an order from the supreme command staff to speed up the process of the interrogation of these people. We said that we were not able to do that, and instead we asked that they be transferred and that then this be done either in Zenica or in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me help you. Do you remember what period of time this was, the relevant period that the judges are asking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this would be in September 1992 -- either August or September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is alright. I will leave the rest for cross-examination. They will be able to find these things out, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have actually concluded my examination of this witness, and I tried to follow your suggestion and directions of yesterday, so that we could at least complete this portion of this witness's testimony before 4 o'clock this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Tahirovic. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I will have a few questions for you, because I can tell that you are very familiar with the situation in Konjic around Konjic and as regards the camp, that is, the prison. Professor, you are professor of All People's Defence and you showed, during your examination, that you are very well versed in military matters; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did Bosnia-Herzegovina have enough time to prepare for its defence in early 1992, given the fact that it did not want the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult and it went with a lot of effort and I believe that we nevertheless were able to prepare, but rather due to the hearts and courage of people rather than materiel and equipment that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How were you able to do so without being attacked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Professor, let me put it this way: was the JNA the body that actually was arming the Serbs in order to carry out its attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers, including the reservists from Serbia and Montenegro did come to Bosnia-Herzegovina after the defeats in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least two corps arrived -- I believe it was one from Slovenia -- it was the so-called 5th or 7th Army District. I think the 5th was in Zagreb, so the entire corps came from Croatia, so, according to the number of personnel that a corps should have, there should have been somewhere between 30,000 and 50,000 people, so one corps is about 17,000 to 20,000 strong and, if you add the reservists from Montenegro who, so to speak, had flooded the whole area at the time, you could probably come up with a figure of 50,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you also say that the JNA did take away weapons from the Territorial Defence, wherever it managed to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We already have enough evidence on that. Witnesses have said from both sides the JNA was arming the local Serbs, the JNA was initially involved in all these -- in the conflict. We already have enough evidence of that. In fact, the experts told us 80,000 troops of the JNA were there until Serbia and Montenegro declared to withdraw from Bosnia, but they left their soldiers of Bosnian extraction there with all the equipment. We already have enough evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. However, this witness is an expert witness, so to speak, because he is a professor of All People's Defence, so is somebody who received his education in the former State, with a very high degree of military expertise, and since part of the indictment concerns the violation of Conventions and the treatment of the prisoners and their status in the prison, I thought that it may be necessary for me to clarify. I am not suggesting that we are hearing this for the first time, but I am trying to elucidate this. Anyway, I am grateful to you for your intervention and I am going to move on to another area. Professor, could we say that the villagers of Bradina and Donje Selo were very well armed, with good quality weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And also very strategic points. We have heard evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (INAUDIBLE) to Sarajevo, Donje Selo and Bradina. Bradina was right there -- I think Mount Igman -- it was a passage. In fact, one of the generals told us that, if you avoid this Igman pass, you have to cross 12 different passes. I think General Divjak told us that. This Donje Selo was controlling the road to Mostar and then probably further on to the sea. We have been educated enough on this matter. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if you will believe me, but I forgot the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The question was, were Donje Selo and Bradina very well armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were very well armed. This morning I said they had mortars, 82-millimetre calibre, which means that they had a complete set of infantry-type weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, since it is 4 o'clock, this might be a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We said yesterday that we will break at 4 o'clock and that we will do that right now. We will reassemble at 4.30 for our status conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Short adjournment) .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will first adjourn the proceedings to 18 May before we start our status conference. It is better that I do that, because I did not indicate the case stands adjourned, so cross-examination will continue on 18 May, for those who have not exercised their right of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be allowed to tell the witness that he is now free and that he may leave the building of the Tribunal, because he waited your decision about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is correct -- I think this is what we will proceed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you -- I will thank him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the usher will definitely go to him and tell him the matter has been adjourned until 18 May. Now we are in closed session for the status conference.
